searchText: Potentially a stupid question -- how are people computing the v value of (v, r, s) in the payload of a signed 1559 transaction? From my understanding, EIP-155 no longer applies because that was defined only for legacy transactions. Is there still guidance (e.g. {0,1} + CHAIN_ID * 2 + 35) on how it should be computed? There is no `v` in 1559 transactions. There is now `yParity`. Apologies, I meant yParity > `YParity` The parity (0 for even, 1 for odd) of the y-value of a secp256k1 signature. Got it, so it's always 0 or 1 Thanks! ChainID is now also part of the transaction, so we no longer have to bitpack it. Hey <@!301186049323958275> quick follow-up - if I have the secp256k1 signature as a hex string, is there a quick way of extracting the y-value (and thereby the parity) from it? Same way you got the `{0,1}` for the `v` previously. There is a fairly standard way of encoding a secp256k1 signature into a byte array, I think two actually: compressed and uncompressed. How many bytes do you have? The signature is 65 bytes https://github.com/Zoltu/ethereum-crypto/blob/master/library/source/secp256k1.ts#L62-L72 Hopefully that gets you close to the answer you seek. You want `affinePoint.y % 2` IIRC. Or maybe the inverse of that? (0 for even, 1 for odd) 🤯 That function returns the 65 byte array you have. So just work backward. kk Looks like the last 32 bytes are the `y` value, and it *appears* (but double check my work) that it is big endian? So maybe you can just `%2` the last byte? That would be ❣️ Yep confirmed - it's big endian so you can just mod the last byte. And the parity seems to be 0 if even, 1 if odd
